entries.title: New Jersey Bans Sale of Sensitive Data and Creates Public Registry for Data Brokers and Collectors
entries.subtitle: New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill signed Assembly Bill 5328 on June 30, 2026, establishing one of the nation's most expansive bans on the sale of sensitive consumer data with a mandatory public registry for data brokers and collectors.
entries.publisher: Ogletree, Deakins, Nash, Smoak & Stewart, P.C.
entries.abstract: Assembly Bill 5328 (A5328), signed into law by New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill on June 30, 2026, prohibits the sale of sensitive consumer data by nearly all individuals and entities, with limited exceptions for HIPAA-covered entities and Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act-covered financial institutions. The legislation defines sensitive data broadly to include information regarding racial or ethnic origin, health conditions, financial account details, sexual orientation, citizenship status, genetic or biometric data, children's data, and precise geolocation data. Violators face civil penalties of $50,000 per record sold or offered for sale. Additionally, A5328 establishes a mandatory public registry requiring data brokers and data collectors to register with the New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs, provide detailed information about their data practices, and pay registration fees ranging from $5,000 to $1,500,000 based on consumer volume, with noncompliance penalties of $2,500 per day.

entries.title: Comparing Recent Federal Data Privacy Bills
entries.subtitle: Analysis of three major federal data privacy legislative proposals from the 117th, 118th, and 119th Congresses.
entries.abstract: This article compares three federal data privacy bills: the American Data Privacy and Protection Act (ADPPA, 2022), the American Privacy Rights Act (APRA, 2024), and the SECURE Data Act (2026). The bills are analyzed across five dimensions: consumer rights, consent requirements, data controller obligations, enforcement mechanisms, and data minimization standards. While all three bills establish similar frameworks for consumer privacy protections, they differ significantly in their prescriptive requirements on data security, consent mechanisms, and the stringency of data minimization standards.

entries.title: Google Beats Suit Over Data Tracking by Gemini AI Assistant
entries.subtitle: A federal judge dismissed a class action lawsuit alleging Google illegally tracked user communications through its Gemini AI assistant, finding plaintiffs failed to establish concrete harm.
entries.abstract: A proposed class action lawsuit against Google alleging that the company used its Gemini AI assistant to illegally track private communications through Gmail, Chat, and Meet was dismissed by Judge Noël Wise of the US District Court for the Northern District of California on July 8, 2026. Plaintiffs Thomas Thele and Melo Porter claimed Google silently enabled the AI tool by default in October 2025 without user consent. The court granted Google's motion to dismiss on standing grounds, finding that plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient concrete harm or specificity regarding the data accessed and their resulting injury, though the judge permitted an amended complaint.

entries.title: New Jersey's Highest-in-Nation Data Broker Fees Shock Industry
entries.subtitle: New Jersey enacted sweeping data broker legislation with registration fees up to $1.5 million annually, the highest in the nation, catching industry stakeholders off-guard due to rapid legislative passage.
entries.abstract: New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill signed into law a data broker regulation on June 30, 2026, establishing annual registration fees ranging from $5,000 to $1.5 million—the highest in the nation—and banning the sale of sensitive personal data. The legislation, introduced and passed within days, uniquely extends regulatory requirements to businesses that collect and sell their own customer data, not just third-party brokers. Industry representatives and privacy advocates expressed surprise at both the bill's rapid passage and its expansive scope, with the measure expected to generate approximately $50 million in revenue to support the state's constitutionally mandated balanced budget.

entries.title: New York Times Seeks Sanctions for OpenAI in Copyright Case
entries.subtitle: The New York Times filed a motion seeking sanctions against OpenAI for allegedly obstructing discovery and concealing the ability to search training data and output logs for copyrighted works over a two-year period.
entries.abstract: In a copyright infringement case consolidated in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, the New York Times Co. and other news publishers have filed a motion seeking sanctions against OpenAI for what they characterize as deliberate obstruction of discovery. The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI concealed its ability to search ChatGPT training data and output logs for copyrighted materials for two years, providing only heavily redacted sample logs that the court deemed unusable. The Times seeks to prohibit OpenAI from relying on the provided output logs, to establish findings regarding systematic copying of news content, and to recover attorneys' fees and expert costs associated with securing the withheld discovery.

entries.title: Agentic AI Liability Fuels Issues Reaching Beyond the Law's Edge
entries.subtitle: As autonomous AI systems take independent actions across the web, courts must grapple with fundamental questions of agency law and liability allocation.
entries.abstract: This commentary examines the emerging legal challenges posed by agentic artificial intelligence systems—autonomous AI that can plan, execute extended interactions, and take real-world actions without continuous human oversight. Using Amazon v. Perplexity AI as a focal point, the author argues that autonomous AI fundamentally challenges traditional common law agency principles, including consent, control, scope of authority, and duty of loyalty. The piece surveys both the technical characteristics of agentic systems and first-generation litigation involving algorithmic decision-making in employment and other contexts, demonstrating how courts will need to reexamine foundational legal premises to allocate liability among AI developers, deployers, and users.

entries.title: AI-Powered Inferred Data Poses New Threats for Consumer Privacy
entries.subtitle: Emerging AI inference tools that generate consumer profiles raise concerns about discrimination, manipulation, and opacity in consequential life decisions.
entries.abstract: This article examines the privacy and discrimination risks posed by AI tools that generate inferences about consumers based on aggregated data, making predictions about sensitive attributes like race, health, and income for use in hiring, lending, housing, and pricing decisions. The piece documents how inference-generating systems create novel harms distinct from traditional data collection, including the challenge that even AI architects may not fully understand how their tools produce outputs. State-level legislative responses, including California's CCPA and recent Maryland and New York laws addressing automated decision-making and surveillance pricing, represent initial policy approaches to address transparency, consent, and consumer rights regarding inferred data.

entries.title: Everything You Need to Know about Knowledge Distillation
entries.subtitle: A comprehensive overview of knowledge distillation techniques, their evolution, and real-world applications following DeepSeek's recent advancements.
entries.abstract: This article examines knowledge distillation (KD), a machine learning technique that transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models. The piece traces KD's evolution from 2006 model compression work through Hinton et al.'s 2015 formalization, explains the mathematical foundations involving softmax and temperature parameters, and discusses various distillation types, scaling laws, benefits, limitations, and contemporary applications including DeepSeek's R1 model distillation.

entries.title: Bank AI Oversight Expands to Every Exam: Generative AI Bypasses SR 26-2 as Kill-Switch Gap Grows
entries.subtitle: Federal banking regulators embed AI governance questions into routine examinations while newly issued guidance excludes generative and agentic AI systems from validation requirements.
entries.abstract: Federal banking regulators have integrated AI governance assessments into all standard bank examinations, focusing on credit decisions, fraud detection, and customer service automation. A survey of 230 banking professionals reveals that nearly 75% of banks lack confidence in their ability to shut down malfunctioning AI systems or report AI failures to regulators. The April 2026 joint guidance (SR 26-2) from the Federal Reserve, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation modernizes model risk management frameworks but explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI—the very systems banks have deployed most aggressively—from validation and documentation requirements.

entries.title: Researchers identify people through ordinary Wi-Fi routers with 99.5% accuracy — technique works with standard Wi-Fi routers
entries.subtitle: Security researchers at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology demonstrate a novel Wi-Fi-based identification attack using beamforming data that achieves unprecedented accuracy without specialized hardware.
entries.abstract: Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology have developed BFId, a technique that exploits unencrypted beamforming feedback information (BFI) broadcast by standard Wi-Fi routers to identify individuals with 99.5% accuracy. Unlike prior Wi-Fi-based identification methods relying on channel state information (CSI), BFId requires no specialized hardware, no network access, and functions regardless of whether targets carry wireless devices. Tested on 197 participants, the technique substantially outperforms existing CSI-based approaches and raises significant privacy concerns, particularly given the recent IEEE 802.11bf standard for Wi-Fi sensing which lacks adequate privacy protections.

entries.title: The Hidden Water Cost of AI: Understanding Infrastructure Impacts Beyond Individual Queries
entries.subtitle: An examination of how artificial intelligence systems consume vast quantities of water globally, with projections showing AI infrastructure could use half of the UK's annual water withdrawal by 2027.
entries.abstract: This article analyzes the water consumption footprint of AI systems, examining both direct cooling-related water use and indirect consumption through electricity generation. While individual AI queries consume modest amounts of water (estimated between five drops and one bottle depending on measurement methodology), cumulative global AI demand is projected to account for 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic meters of water withdrawal by 2027. The piece discusses methodological differences between major studies and emphasizes that water use varies significantly by geographic location, data center infrastructure, and accounting frameworks.

entries.title: Mayor Mamdani Announces Landmark "Click-To-Cancel" Consumer Protection Rules to Ban Subscription Traps and Junk Fees
entries.subtitle: New York City announces first-in-nation municipal regulations requiring transparent all-in pricing and easy subscription cancellation mechanisms.
entries.publisher: Office of the Mayor, New York City
entries.abstract: New York City has announced comprehensive consumer protection regulations addressing subscription traps and hidden junk fees. The rules include a proposed transparent all-in pricing requirement banning hidden mandatory charges and a final click-to-cancel rule requiring subscription cancellation to be as simple as sign-up. The city estimates the click-to-cancel rule alone will save New Yorkers approximately $162.5 million annually, with families currently paying an average of $3,200 per year in hidden fees. These regulations represent significant municipal consumer protection policy and address market failures in digital commerce and subscription services.

entries.title: Built for Speed: The Hidden Costs of Last-Mile Delivery
entries.subtitle: An analysis of how speed-driven logistics systems generate occupational hazards for last-mile delivery drivers through fragmented responsibility and algorithmic control.
entries.abstract: This article examines the structural risks embedded in last-mile delivery systems, arguing that workplace hazards emerge from the interaction of speed optimization, algorithmic management, and fragmented responsibility. The author demonstrates how logistics firms maintain operational control over delivery pace and performance metrics while distributing legal accountability across networks of third-party contractors, leaving drivers to bear safety risks without traditional employment protections. Current regulatory frameworks fail to address the distinctive hazards of urban delivery work, creating a policy gap that leaves workers insufficiently protected.

entries.title: Protecting Kids Online: Government Mandates vs. Market Solutions
entries.subtitle: An analysis of how proposed legislative knowledge standards for user age verification could create unintended privacy and speech consequences for digital platforms and users.
entries.abstract: This policy analysis examines legislative proposals that would modify how digital platforms must verify user age, particularly through heightened "constructive knowledge" standards that effectively mandate age verification. The paper argues that while intended to protect minors, such requirements would necessitate collection of personally identifiable information and biometric data, creating privacy risks for both adult and minor users, potential data breach vulnerabilities, and chilling effects on speech. The analysis reviews various legislative approaches including KOSA, COPPA 2.0, KIDS Act, and ASAA, comparing the tradeoffs between child safety protections and privacy, innovation, and civil liberties concerns.

entries.title: CPU vs GPU vs TPU vs NPU: AI Hardware Processing Units Explained
entries.subtitle: A comprehensive guide to AI hardware architectures comparing traditional processors, specialized accelerators, and emerging custom-built chips.
entries.abstract: This article provides a technical overview of processing unit architectures used in AI systems, examining the fundamental differences between Central Processing Units (CPUs), Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), and specialized alternatives. The piece traces the historical development of CPU technology from ENIAC through modern multi-core processors, explains the computational strengths and limitations of each architecture type, and surveys emerging alternatives including ASICs, APUs, NPUs, IPUs, and FPGAs. The analysis emphasizes that while GPUs have dominated AI infrastructure discourse, alternative hardware designs offer distinct efficiencies and approaches for different computational workloads.

entries.title: It is time to restore the US Office of Technology Assessment
entries.subtitle: A policy brief arguing for the reinstatement of Congress's defunct technology assessment agency to address emerging digital governance challenges.
entries.abstract: This policy brief examines the 1995 elimination of the U.S. Office of Technology Assessment (OTA) by the Republican-controlled Congress and argues for its restoration in light of contemporary technology governance challenges. The author contends that Congress lacks adequate institutional capacity to conduct impartial analysis of rapidly evolving digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, autonomous vehicles, and algorithmic systems. The piece identifies gaps in current policy advisory structures and recommends establishing a dedicated, nonpartisan body to provide objective research and analysis on technology's societal impacts.

entries.title: Meta Layoff Bias Suit Exposes Employer Risk in AI Firing Factors
entries.subtitle: A lawsuit against Meta demonstrates legal vulnerabilities when companies use AI systems to make employment termination decisions without accounting for protected leave and disabilities.
entries.abstract: A lawsuit filed against Meta Platforms Inc. by 26 former and current workers alleges the company used AI systems to discriminatorily rank and select employees for layoffs without considering how protected leave or disabilities influenced performance metrics. The case represents one of the first major legal challenges to AI use in employee termination decisions and exposes employers to liability under multiple legal frameworks including Title VII, the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and California's 2025 AI employment regulations. The dispute centers on whether Meta's AI systems improperly weighted factors such as AI usage and productivity metrics that would necessarily disadvantage workers on medical or disability leave, raising broader questions about how employers can lawfully incorporate AI into employment decisions.

entries.title: America Needs One National Framework for Artificial Intelligence
entries.subtitle: Two members of Congress propose a bipartisan legislative framework to establish uniform national AI governance standards while protecting innovation and workers.
entries.abstract: Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) introduce the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, a bipartisan discussion draft proposing a unified national framework for AI regulation. The proposal addresses safety requirements for frontier AI systems, labor market impact monitoring, workforce development, and international competitiveness, while avoiding state-by-state regulatory fragmentation. The framework includes mandatory safety plans and incident reporting for large developers, independent auditing mechanisms, federal data collection on AI's employment effects, and investments in AI education and workforce preparation.

entries.title: How Personalization Drives Consumer Choice and Autonomy
entries.subtitle: An examination of how AI-driven personalization technologies can be governed to enhance consumer welfare while maintaining transparency and competition.
entries.abstract: This article analyzes the evolution of personalization in digital systems, particularly as driven by advanced AI technologies that integrate across multiple platforms and services. The author argues that while personalization creates legitimate data governance concerns, it also delivers substantial consumer value by reducing information overload and search costs. The piece contends that policy frameworks should regulate harmful outcomes such as fraud and deception rather than restrict core technology features, and that overly strict regulatory approaches may inadvertently concentrate market power and delay innovation.

entries.title: Breaking the optical barrier: Terahertz tech could help enable quantum internet security
entries.subtitle: University of Glasgow researchers propose terahertz-based quantum key distribution as a secure alternative to conventional optical QKD systems.
entries.abstract: Researchers at the University of Glasgow have developed a simulation-based approach to quantum key distribution (QKD) using terahertz waves transmitted through wireless communications systems adapted from mobile and WiFi networks. The proposed system employs superconducting Josephson junction coherent emitters and Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) to enable secure quantum communication across multiple environments, including open air (4 meters), space (100+ kilometers), and cryogenically-cooled cables (26 kilometers). This work presents a high-fidelity, energy-efficient alternative to laser-based and fiber-optic QKD infrastructure, with potential applications in future quantum internet security.

entries.title: LeJEPA: Provable and Scalable Self-Supervised Learning Without the Heuristics
entries.subtitle: Yann LeCun's new theoretically grounded JEPA variant introduces SIGReg regularization to stabilize representation learning and prevent embedding collapse.
entries.abstract: LeJEPA is a self-supervised learning architecture that provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), a framework proposed by Yann LeCun in 2022. The model addresses representation collapse through SIGReg, a Gaussian regularization method that enforces isotropic Gaussian distributions in learned embeddings without relying on fragile heuristics. This work positions JEPA-style world models as a practical foundation for embodied AI, robotics, and predictive systems across multiple modalities.

entries.title: Why community benefit agreements are necessary for data centers
entries.subtitle: AI companies should establish legally binding community benefit agreements with local leaders to address public concerns about data center construction and operations.
entries.abstract: Data centers are essential infrastructure for AI and the digital economy, yet their construction has faced significant public opposition across the United States due to concerns about energy costs, environmental impact, and corporate power. The authors argue that community benefit agreements (CBAs)—formal, legally binding documents negotiated collaboratively between developers and host communities—can mitigate these concerns by providing transparency about costs, benefits, and long-term impacts. CBAs should include quantifiable data on job creation, tax revenue, workforce training, and health contributions, along with rigorous evaluation mechanisms to ensure mutual respect and accountability between all parties.

entries.title: After a $16 billion Stargate AI data center was built despite being voted down, Michigan towns rush to block new buildouts — massive facility will suck 1.4 Gigawatts of energy to power ChatGPT
entries.subtitle: Michigan municipalities implement data center moratoriums in response to the Stargate facility's approval despite local opposition and concerns over energy consumption and resource use.
entries.abstract: Following the approval and construction of Oracle and OpenAI's $16 billion Stargate data center in Saline Township despite near-unanimous local opposition, at least 19 Michigan municipalities have enacted moratoriums on new data center development. The facility, which will consume 1.4 gigawatts of electricity, was advanced through litigation after a developer sued the township for allegedly exclusionary zoning, resulting in a settlement that secured $14 million in community benefits. The backlash has expanded to include county-level resolutions, bipartisan state legislative proposals for a temporary statewide pause, and regional water authority restrictions, reflecting broader concerns about AI infrastructure development and its environmental and fiscal impacts on local communities.

entries.title: Uber caps employee AI spending after blowing through budget in 4 months
entries.subtitle: Uber implements monthly per-employee AI usage caps following rapid depletion of annual budget, raising questions about enterprise AI return on investment.
entries.abstract: Uber Technologies has instituted internal usage caps limiting employee spending on agentic coding tools to $1,500 per month per employee, following the company's depletion of its entire annual AI budget within four months. The cost control measure reflects broader industry concerns regarding the return on investment from enterprise AI spending, particularly as companies struggle to demonstrate clear productivity gains from increased AI tool adoption. Uber's experience, which included internal gamification of AI usage through competitive leaderboards, illustrates the tension between aggressive AI adoption strategies and fiscal sustainability.

entries.title: Social Media Addiction Lawsuits (2026): KGM Trial, MDL 3047, and TikTok & Snapchat Settlements Explained
entries.subtitle: An examination of mass tort litigation against social media platforms for allegedly addictive design targeting minors, with the first bellwether trial underway as of March 2026.
entries.abstract: This article provides comprehensive analysis of social media addiction mass tort litigation, comparing it to landmark tobacco lawsuits. The litigation alleges that platforms including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube employ deliberately addictive design features targeting children and adolescents. The article examines core allegations, specific design mechanics, novel legal strategies circumventing Section 230 immunity, and First Amendment defenses, with particular focus on the active KGM v. Meta & YouTube bellwether trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.

entries.title: Legal Policies on Platform Liability: An Economic Approach
entries.subtitle: An economic analysis of how holding online platforms accountable for third-party seller defects affects consumer welfare, seller incentives, and market efficiency.
entries.abstract: This paper examines the evolving legal landscape of platform liability for defective products sold through online marketplaces like Amazon and Airbnb, using the Oberdorf v. Amazon case as a primary example. The authors present a theoretical economic model to assess how increased platform liability impacts seller behavior, consumer welfare, and market efficiency, finding that liability effects vary significantly depending on product value. The analysis reveals that while platform liability can enhance consumer compensation, it may reduce sellers' safety investment incentives for low-value goods while potentially improving safety outcomes for high-value goods.

entries.title: How do recommender systems work on digital platforms?
entries.subtitle: An examination of how recommender systems have become central to information distribution and the mechanisms underlying modern recommendation algorithms.
entries.abstract: This article traces the evolution of recommender systems on digital platforms, from simple reverse-chronological feeds to complex deep learning models. It explains why platforms have progressively adopted more sophisticated algorithmic approaches to content curation and identifies the fundamental tradeoffs between performance, cost, and interpretability. The piece argues that recommender systems now function as critical infrastructure for democratic information flow, necessitating informed oversight from policymakers and researchers.

entries.title: The Guardian, Wired, TIME, and The Atlantic Are All Collaborating with OpenAI
entries.subtitle: A comprehensive analysis of media outlets' commercial partnerships with OpenAI and implications for journalistic independence and AI model training.
entries.abstract: This commentary documents the proliferation of content licensing agreements between major news organizations and OpenAI, detailing which outlets have granted the company access to their archives for model training and product enhancement. The author identifies over 30 publications across multiple media conglomerates—including The Guardian, TIME, The Atlantic, Wired, and others—that have entered into strategic partnerships with OpenAI. The piece raises concerns about media independence, lack of public awareness regarding these arrangements, and the absence of author opt-out provisions in standard publishing contracts that enable AI companies to use copyrighted content for training purposes.

entries.title: DeepMind slows down research releases to keep competitive edge in AI race
entries.abstract: DeepMind has implemented a more restrictive publication policy, including six-month embargoes on strategic generative AI papers and increased bureaucratic review processes, according to seven current and former research scientists. The shift represents a significant departure from DeepMind's historical commitment to releasing groundbreaking research for public benefit, driven by competitive pressures and Google's effort to monetize AI breakthroughs. The company has blocked papers revealing vulnerabilities in competitors' models and comparative analyses of its own Gemini model, causing concern among researchers for whom publication success is a critical career metric.

entries.title: For now, Live Nation deal is just a Band Aid, says antitrust scholar
entries.subtitle: Harvard Law visiting professor Rebecca Haw Allensworth discusses the DOJ's settlement with Live Nation Entertainment and why the deal falls short of addressing underlying anti-competitive concerns.
entries.abstract: This interview examines the March 2026 settlement between the DOJ and Live Nation Entertainment, which resolved antitrust litigation without requiring the breakup of Live Nation and Ticketmaster that the government initially sought. The scholar argues that while the settlement imposes restrictions on exclusive booking arrangements and caps ticketing fees at 15 percent for amphitheaters, these measures represent a superficial remedy that fails to address the core problem of vertical integration across ticketing, venue ownership, and concert promotion markets. The settlement allows Live Nation to maintain monopolistic power and shift profits across vertically integrated business lines, potentially limiting competitive entry and consumer benefits.

entries.title: The future of data centers
entries.subtitle: An examination of data center infrastructure requirements, challenges, and policy considerations for supporting AI growth and economic competitiveness.
entries.abstract: This article analyzes the critical role of data centers in enabling artificial intelligence applications across multiple sectors. The authors examine infrastructure challenges including energy and water consumption, critical mineral requirements, workforce shortages, permitting barriers, and electric grid investment needs. The analysis addresses financial costs, job market impacts, national security considerations, and geographical distribution strategies necessary for ensuring sustained digital economy transition while maintaining U.S. international competitiveness.

entries.title: Eli Lilly, InSilico Strike AI Drug Discovery Deal
entries.abstract: Eli Lilly announced a drug discovery partnership with Hong Kong-listed InSilico valued at up to $2.75 billion, comprising a $115 million upfront payment and milestone-based compensation. Under the agreement, InSilico will grant Lilly exclusive worldwide rights to oral treatments developed using its Pharma.AI artificial intelligence platform across multiple therapeutic areas. This deal extends an existing partnership begun in 2023 and reflects a broader trend among global pharmaceutical companies establishing licensing agreements and major investments in China's increasingly competitive drug innovation sector.

entries.title: To repeal or not to repeal is not the question for Section 230
entries.abstract: This piece examines the debate surrounding Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act and argues against its repeal as a solution to online harms. The author contends that repealing Section 230 would not effectively address concerns about harmful content and platform accountability because much of the problematic speech remains constitutionally protected. Instead, the author proposes targeted structural reforms including enhanced transparency requirements, privacy protections, researcher access safeguards, and user data portability that would address underlying concerns without incentivizing platforms to suppress lawful speech or concentrating further power among large platforms.

entries.title: Walmart Is Putting Digital Labels that Change Prices Instantly on Every Store Shelf in America
entries.subtitle: Walmart's rollout of digital shelf labels creates technological infrastructure that could enable dynamic pricing in grocery retail, raising consumer protection concerns.
entries.abstract: Walmart announced plans to deploy digital shelf labels (DSLs) across all U.S. stores by end of 2026, replacing paper price tags with remotely updatable digital displays. While marketed as a labor-efficiency measure, DSLs remove the operational friction that previously constrained frequent price changes, making dynamic pricing technically feasible in grocery retail. The article examines how this capability differs from existing dynamic pricing in airlines and hotels, discusses the distinct social contract governing grocery pricing, and references consumer backlash against Wendy's dynamic pricing announcement as evidence of market resistance to such practices.

entries.title: The Game Theory of How Algorithms Can Drive Up Prices
entries.subtitle: Learning algorithms may achieve tacit collusion and high prices without explicit coordination or threat mechanisms, posing novel regulatory challenges.
entries.excerpt: Machine learning algorithms used for dynamic pricing can unexpectedly converge on collusive outcomes without any explicit coordination — learning to implement mutual retaliation strategies similar to human cartels. The findings expose a gap in antitrust enforcement frameworks designed to detect explicit agreements, not emergent algorithmic behavior.
entries.abstract: This article examines how machine learning algorithms used for dynamic pricing can unexpectedly converge on collusive pricing outcomes without explicit programming or coordination. Recent research demonstrates that algorithms can learn to implement implicit threats and mutual retaliation strategies similar to human cartels, and that even benign profit-optimizing algorithms may produce supracompetitive prices.
